result.summary: The battle turns against the Trojans until Helenus sends Hector to the city to organise prayers to Minerva. On the field Glaucus and Diomed discover an old family friendship and exchange armour. Hector then meets Hecuba, rebukes Paris, speaks with Helen, and takes a tender farewell of Andromache and their son before returning to battle with Paris.

scenes.title: Slaughter on the plain
scenes.summary: Achaeans kill many Trojans. Agamemnon talks Menelaus out of sparing Adrestus, and Nestor urges the men to keep killing rather than looting.
scenes.stakes: Adrestus pleads for his life; the Trojans risk being routed and destroyed.

scenes.title: Helenus sends Hector to Troy
scenes.summary: Helenus tells Hector and Aeneas to rally the troops, and sends Hector to have the women pray to Minerva. Hector rallies the Trojans and leaves for the city.
scenes.stakes: The Trojans fear Diomed's fury and the fall of their city.

scenes.title: Diomed challenges Glaucus
scenes.summary: Diomed asks who Glaucus is, warning that he will not fight a god, and recalls the fate of Lycurgus. Glaucus replies that men are like leaves.
scenes.stakes: Glaucus faces single combat with the fiercest Achaean.

scenes.title: The story of Bellerophon
scenes.summary: Glaucus tells how Bellerophon was slandered by Antea, sent to Lycia with a deadly letter, and survived the Chimaera, Solymi, Amazons and an ambush. He married the king's daughter.
scenes.stakes: Bellerophon is to be killed through the king's schemes.

scenes.title: Exchange of armour
scenes.summary: Diomed realises their families are guest-friends, and they agree to avoid each other and swap armour. Jove addles Glaucus into a bad trade.

scenes.title: Prayer to Minerva in Troy
scenes.summary: Hector meets the Trojan women and Hecuba, who gathers the matrons and brings a robe to Minerva's temple. Theano prays, but Minerva refuses.
scenes.stakes: The city of Troy is threatened by Diomed.

scenes.title: Hector rebukes Paris
scenes.summary: Hector finds Paris with his armour and scolds him. Helen blames herself, and Hector declines to sit and goes to see his family.
scenes.stakes: Troy is at risk because Paris holds back from the fight.

scenes.title: Hector and Andromache
scenes.summary: At the Scaean gates Andromache begs Hector to stay, recounting her lost family. Hector refuses, foresees Troy's fall, and prays for his son Astyanax, who is frightened by his helmet.
scenes.stakes: Hector may die, leaving Andromache a widow or captive and their son fatherless.

scenes.title: Paris rejoins Hector
scenes.summary: Paris hurries through the city like a horse set free and meets Hector. They go back to the battle.

alias_notes.explanation: Hector named him Scamandrius, but people called him Astyanax, 'lord of the city'.

notable_quotes.reason: Glaucus's famous comparison of human generations to leaves.
Hector tells Andromache that war is men's business.
Hector foresees Troy's fall and fears most for Andromache's captivity.

analysis.text: The book contrasts the code of heroic glory with family love, most clearly in Hector's farewell to Andromache. Glaucus's leaves speech reflects on mortality.
The guest-friendship of Glaucus and Diomed shows how xenia bonds could override the loyalties of war in the heroic world.

legacy.text: Glaucus's comparison of generations to leaves was echoed by later poets, including Virgil and Milton.
The phrase 'Glaucus and Diomed' exchange, gold for bronze, became a proverb for a lopsided bargain.

fun_facts.text: Bellerophon's letter that carries his own death sentence is one of the earliest references to writing in Greek literature.

language_notes.text: Simois and Xanthus are the two rivers of the Trojan plain; Xanthus is also called Scamander. They mark the battlefield's bounds.
"Stood before him" means stood up in his defence; none of his guests protected him from death.
"Had converse with" is a polite archaic phrase meaning he slept with the nymph.
"The son of Mecisteus" is Euryalus, named earlier in sentence 5.
Ransom: payment offered by a captive's family for his release, a common custom in the poem.
"Giving quarter" means showing mercy by sparing a defeated enemy's life.
Agamemnon alludes to the wrong done to Menelaus when Paris took Helen, the cause of the war.
"Spoil the dead" means strip fallen enemies of armour and goods; booty is the plunder taken.
Augurs were priests who interpreted omens, especially bird signs. Helenus is called wisest of them, which explains why his advice carries authority.
Ilius is another name for Troy (Ilium), the city the Trojans are defending.
"Upon the knees of Minerva" refers to the seated cult statue of the goddess; the robe is laid on its lap as an offering.
"Never yet felt the goad" means the heifers are unbroken and unworked, so they are pure and fit for sacrifice.
A hecatomb was a large sacrifice of cattle, originally a hundred, offered to the gods.
Hector's large body-shield has a dark hide rim that knocks against his neck and ankles as he walks.
Thyrsi are staffs wreathed in ivy and topped with a pine cone, carried by followers of Bacchus (the Greek Dionysus).
"The son of Saturn" is Jove (Zeus), king of the gods, here punishing Lycurgus.
"Eat the fruit of the ground" means mortal, as opposed to gods who live on ambrosia and nectar.
Ephyra is an ancient name for Corinth. Sisyphus, its founder, was famous for cunning and was later punished in the underworld by endlessly rolling a stone uphill.
The 'lying letters' on a folded tablet are the 'Bellerophontic letter': a message that secretly orders the bearer's death. This is a rare reference to writing in Homer.
'Rosy-fingered morning' is Homer's stock description of dawn, repeated throughout the poem.
'To have and to hold' is a formal legal phrase for lasting possession, here used for the land grant.
'Lay with' means had sexual relations with. Jove fathering Sarpedon makes him a demigod who fights at Troy.
Bellerophon, a Greek hero, was hosted by Oeneus, Diomed's grandfather. Glaucus is Bellerophon's grandson, so their families are bound by guest-friendship (xenia), which forbids fighting.
Refers to the expedition of the Seven against Thebes, in which Diomed's father Tydeus died.
"Middle Argos" means the heart of the Argive land; "plighted friendship" in the next line means pledged it solemnly.
"Take leave of his wits" means Jove made Glaucus lose his judgment, so he accepted a absurdly unequal trade.
The Scaean gates were the main gate of Troy; the oak tree beside them was a known landmark.
"Driver of the spoil" is an epithet of Minerva, probably meaning she drives off or leads plunder. "Goad" is a stick for driving cattle.
Alexandrus is another name for Paris. His voyage to Sparta and abduction of Helen caused the war.
"Pallas" is a title often attached to Minerva (the Greek Athena).
The Trojan women are praying to Minerva (the Greek Athena), daughter of Jove, in the preceding scene; Hector goes to Alexandrus meanwhile.
A cubit was about the length of a forearm, roughly 18 inches, so the spear is around 16 feet long, a heroic size.
Cuirass: armour protecting the chest and back. Argive here means Greek, and Helen is called so because she came from Greece.
Rancour means bitter resentment. Hector suspects Alexandrus is sulking and holding back out of anger.
Alexandrus claims grief, not ill-will, keeps him at home. This is a weak excuse that Hector does not answer.
Helen wishes she had been carried off by a storm at birth, before the mischief of the war began.
Helen foresees that she and Paris will become subjects of song, as the Iliad itself does.
"Propitiating" means appeasing or winning the favour of the goddess, here through prayer and offerings.
Scaean gates: the main gate of Troy, facing the plain where the fighting takes place.
Astyanax means roughly "lord of the city"; the name reflects Hector's role as Troy's defender.
A barrow is a burial mound; burning the dead in full armour was an honour Achilles gave Eetion.
Being taken by Diana's arrows is the poem's way of saying she died suddenly and gently.
Andromache lists Greek leaders who have already probed the wall's weak spot by the fig-tree.
Argos here stands for Greece generally; Messeis and Hypereia are springs in Greek lands where captive women would draw water.
A distaff is a staff holding wool for spinning, a symbol of women's household work.
"Set the cup of our deliverance" means to hold a victory feast, offering a mixing-bowl libation to the gods.

context_notes.text: Laomedon was an earlier king of Troy and father of Priam, so these slain twins are Priam's kin.
Menelaus, king of Sparta and Agamemnon's brother, is the husband of Helen, whose abduction began the war.
Nestor is the oldest Achaean leader, respected for his counsel. Argives and Danaans are other names for the Achaeans; Mars is the war god.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) was protector of cities and a patron of warriors, so the Trojan women appeal to her for protection against Diomed.
The Achaeans, Danaans and Argives are all names for the Greeks.
Glaucus is a Lycian ally of Troy; Diomed, son of Tydeus, is a Greek champion at the height of his fighting.
Thetis is a sea goddess and the mother of Achilles.
Proetus ruled Argos and Tiryns. Bellerophon had come to him as an exile after killing a man, so he was a guest under his protection.
The Chimaera was a fire-breathing hybrid monster. In later tradition Bellerophon killed it riding the winged horse Pegasus, which Homer does not mention here.
The Amazons were a legendary nation of warrior women, often placed on the edges of the known world.
Mars (the Greek Ares) is the god of war, and Diana (Artemis) the goddess of hunting. Both are known for sudden, violent deaths.
Greeks held that blood-stained hands made a man ritually impure, so he could not make offerings to the gods.
Hector blames Paris, whose abduction of Helen brought the war upon Troy.
Antenor was a respected Trojan elder; his wife Theano serves as Minerva's priestess.
The acropolis is Troy's fortified high citadel, where the royal family lived close together.
Alexandrus is another name for Paris, whose abduction of Helen caused the war.
Hector's wife is Andromache and his son is Astyanax. He is going to see them before returning to battle.
Eetion's city Thebe in the Troad was sacked by Achilles earlier in the war, before the events of the poem.
Achilles, the greatest Greek warrior, is now absent from the fighting because of his quarrel with Agamemnon.
Greek helmets had crests of horse-hair, which could look terrifying to a small child.
Paris, whose abduction of Helen caused the war, had been criticised by Hector for lingering away from battle.

literary_notes.text: The battle is pictured as a tide surging back and forth, conveying its shifting, overwhelming force.
"Tower of strength" characterises Ajax as a steadfast defender of the Achaeans.
Axylus's famed hospitality to all passersby cannot save him; his kindness contrasts bitterly with his death.
Agamemnon's call to kill even unborn children exaggerates to show his ruthless, total hatred of Troy.
Agamemnon personally kills the suppliant, showing his harshness and his dominance over his brother.
Helenus shows how terrifying Diomed is by saying the Trojans fear him even more than Achilles, a goddess's son.
The Greeks think a god has aided the Trojans, when it is only Hector's leadership that has rallied them.
Diomed's tale of Lycurgus serves as a mythic warning about the danger of fighting gods, and sets up his cautious question.
Human generations are compared to leaves, which fall and return, expressing the brevity and renewal of mortal life.
The detailed description of the Chimaera's composite body makes the task seem near-impossible, which raises Bellerophon's stature as a hero.
The king's attempts to destroy Bellerophon have the opposite effect: each failure proves his worth and wins him a wife, land and honour.
'Gnawing at his own heart' expresses Bellerophon's despair as self-consuming grief, a vivid image of melancholy.
Glaucus ends his long digression by tying it back to his purpose, presenting his lineage as proof of his worth as a warrior.
The narrator contrasts the gold and bronze values sharply, making the exchange a famous example of folly caused by divine interference.
Hector's wish that the earth swallow Paris expresses his bitter anger at his brother.
The robe glittering like a star conveys its splendor and makes it a worthy offering.
The goddess's refusal, stated flatly, hints at Troy's eventual doom.
The gleaming bronze point and gold ring give a vivid picture of Hector as a splendid warrior.
Alexandrus shifts blame onto his wife and speaks lightly of victory, showing his evasive, unreliable character.
Helen's blunt contempt for Alexandrus shows her clear-eyed and self-critical nature, and the proverb-like ending adds irony.
Hector's doubt that he will return hints at his eventual death at the hands of the Achaeans.
Comparing the baby to a star conveys his beauty and brightness, and hints at fragile, doomed promise.
Hector foresees Troy's fall and Andromache's captivity, anticipating events beyond the poem's own ending.
The nodding plume frightening the baby sets warrior's fierceness against fatherly tenderness in a vivid, humanizing moment.
The household mourns Hector while he lives, tragically anticipating his death in Book 22.
Paris is likened to a spirited horse breaking free, showing his vigour and showy confidence, in contrast to Hector's gravity.
